patient.chief_complaint: Sudden left arm and leg weakness
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Everett is a 41-year-old right-handed African American man who is a freelance jazz saxophonist, presenting to the emergency department via EMS with acute-onset left-sided weakness beginning approximately 3 hours ago. He was at home preparing for an evening performance when he suddenly noticed his left arm felt heavy and clumsy. Within minutes, his left leg became weak and he was unable to stand without support. His roommate, who was visiting, called 911. On further history, the patient reports that for the past 6 weeks he has been experiencing intermittent low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue, poor appetite, and an unintentional 8 kg weight loss. He attributed these symptoms to his demanding performance schedule and a persistent 'flu' that he could not shake. He notes generalized joint aches, particularly in his knees and wrists, that began approximately 4 weeks ago. Two weeks ago he noticed painful red bumps on the pads of his left index and middle fingers, which he thought were from playing saxophone. He also noticed small dark streaks under his fingernails. He has not sought medical attention for these symptoms. He had a dental extraction 8 weeks ago that was complicated by prolonged bleeding, for which he was prescribed amoxicillin for 7 days but took only 3 days of the course. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve discovered 5 years ago, which he was told was benign and required no treatment or follow-up. He explicitly denies any intravenous drug use, past or present. He denies chest pain, frank dyspnea, or lower extremity edema, though he has noticed becoming winded more easily during saxophone performances in the past few weeks. He has had no prior strokes, seizures, or neurological symptoms.

output.proposed: IV alteplase (tPA) 0.9 mg/kg for acute ischemic stroke
interactions: Ibuprofen (NSAID): antiplatelet effect raises bleeding risk but is not the limiting factor here.
contraindications: Acute ischemic stroke attributable to infective endocarditis is a contraindication to IV alteplase: thrombolysis markedly increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage and rupture of associated mycotic (infectious) aneurysms (AHA/ASA 2019, Class III - Harm).
warnings: Systemic anticoagulation is also generally avoided in the acute phase of infective-endocarditis stroke because of hemorrhagic-transformation and mycotic-aneurysm rupture risk.
Confirm blood cultures and echocardiography before committing to an antithrombotic strategy; vascular imaging should screen for mycotic aneurysms.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast CT must precede any thrombolysis decision; in suspected IE, tPA is generally contraindicated regardless.
Blood cultures should be drawn BEFORE empiric antibiotics to maximize yield for endocarditis diagnosis.
TEE to identify vegetations and assess valvular involvement informs both surgical urgency and antithrombotic decisions.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Apply Duke criteria — major (positive blood cultures, echo vegetation) + minor (predisposing valve, fever, embolic phenomena) define IE
Draw three sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE empiric antibiotics
Obtain transesophageal echocardiogram urgently — TTE alone misses ~30% of vegetations
Screen for mycotic aneurysms with MRA/CTA before any anticoagulation or thrombolysis
Consult cardiothoracic surgery early — valve replacement may be required for large vegetations, refractory infection, perivalvular abscess, or recurrent embolism
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not administer IV tPA in known or strongly suspected infective endocarditis — hemorrhagic complications are unacceptably high
Do not start empiric anticoagulation in IE-related stroke without confirming absence of mycotic aneurysm and weighing hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not initiate antibiotics before blood cultures are drawn, except in hemodynamic instability

Avoid check_drug_interactions with proposed=alteplase: IV alteplase is contraindicated in known/suspected infective endocarditis due to high hemorrhagic transformation and mycotic aneurysm rupture risk — antibiotic and antithrombotic decisions must take this into account
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Fever + new neurologic deficit + structurally abnormal valve (bicuspid aortic) + recent dental procedure pattern matches infective endocarditis with cerebral embolism
Multiple acute infarcts in multiple territories on DWI strongly favor embolic mechanism and warrant aggressive embolic source workup
Mycotic aneurysms (typically distal MCA) are silent until they rupture catastrophically — vessel imaging is mandatory before anticoagulation
TEE is mandatory when IE is suspected and TTE is non-diagnostic — sensitivity for posterior valve vegetations is significantly higher
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — 41-year-old musician with subacute constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) now presenting with acute MCA stroke. Multi-territory infarcts on MRI reveal an embolic shower. The underlying diagnosis is infective endocarditis on a bicuspid aortic valve (Streptococcus mutans from incomplete dental antibiotic prophylaxis). Requires recognizing systemic signs of endocarditis, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics, avoiding thrombolysis, and monitoring for mycotic aneurysm.
clinical_pearls: Multi-territory bilateral brain infarcts on DWI MRI is the imaging hallmark of endocarditis-related embolic shower and should trigger immediate cardiac evaluation
IV tPA is contraindicated in endocarditis-related stroke — hemorrhagic transformation rates from septic vasculopathy and mycotic aneurysm rupture approach 20-40% in published case series
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly (1-2% of the population) and carries a 20x increased risk of infective endocarditis

The modified Duke criteria require a combination of major and minor criteria: positive blood cultures with typical organism + echocardiographic evidence constitute 2 major criteria (definite endocarditis)
Mycotic aneurysms develop in 2-10% of endocarditis cases with CNS embolization and may not be present on initial imaging — serial MRA/CTA surveillance is essential
